html:
The sixteen "great realms" of north India, kingdoms and aristocratic republics that existed from about the 6th to the 4th century BCE. Their world is the world of the Buddha and Mahavira.

Buddhist texts list them: Anga, Magadha, Kashi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Surasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja. Most lay along the Ganges plain. Some were monarchies. Others, like the Vajji league of the Licchavis, were republics ruled by assemblies of clan leaders; the Buddha's own Shakya clan was a small republic of this kind.

This was India's "second urbanisation", a thousand years after the Indus cities. Iron tools cleared forest, rice fed growing towns, and the first Indian coins, punch-marked silver pieces, came into use. With the cities came new thinkers who questioned the priests and sacrifices of the Vedic tradition, among them the Buddhists, the Jains and the Ajivikas.

The realms fought constantly, and the big ones swallowed the small. Magadha won:

  • King Bimbisara annexed Anga.
  • His son Ajatashatru conquered Kosala and the Vajji republic, and fortified the village that became Pataliputra.
  • The Nanda dynasty then built a large, rich state across the Ganges plain.

In the northwest, Gandhara fell under the Persian Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander reached the Punjab in 326 BCE. Around 322 BCE Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas and founded the Maurya Empire.
sum: The sixteen "great realms" of north India, kingdoms and aristocratic republics that existed from about the 6th to the 4th century BCE. Their world is the world of the Buddha and Mahavira.
